- Do not sign at the door. Doorknocking and high pressure phone sales are still common in regional towns.
- Ask what happens to your existing hot water and whether the roof needs work first. Putting panels on a roof that needs replacing in four years is an expensive mistake.
- Get the warranty terms for the panels, the inverter and the installation workmanship as three separate figures, and find out who honours each one.

Start with [solar installers](/categories/solar-installers/), or the local listings for [electricians in Wodonga](/vic/wodonga/electricians/) if the job is a battery or switchboard upgrade alongside the panels.

faqs.q: How much is the solar rebate right now?
faqs.a: There is no single figure, and any number quoted here would go stale. The federal certificate discount changes with the market price of certificates and falls each year as the scheme runs down, and state programs change their amounts and eligibility regularly. Check the Clean Energy Regulator page for the federal scheme and Solar Victoria or the New South Wales energy pages for state programs.

faqs.q: Is the federal scheme a rebate I claim afterwards?
faqs.a: No. It is a certificate scheme, and in practice you assign the certificates to your installer or retailer who takes the value off the invoice. You see it as a discount on the quoted price rather than a payment. That is why quotes are usually shown as the price after certificates.

faqs.q: Does New South Wales have a household solar rebate like Victoria?
faqs.a: Not in the same form. New South Wales has generally delivered incentives through industry schemes such as the Peak Demand Reduction Scheme and the Energy Savings Scheme, where accredited providers pass on a discount, rather than through a single household rebate you apply for. Programs open and close, so check the current New South Wales Government energy pages.

faqs.q: Why does my quote say I can only export 5 kilowatts?
faqs.a: Because the network distributor sets export limits, and they depend on the local network, your phase configuration and sometimes the specific feeder. Essential Energy covers most of regional New South Wales, with AusNet and Powercor covering most of regional Victoria. The installer should confirm your export limit in writing before you sign.

faqs.q: Do I have to apply for a state rebate before installing?
faqs.a: Usually yes. State programs typically require an eligibility application and an approval before the installation goes ahead, and they require the installer to be on an approved list. Signing a contract or installing first can make you ineligible, so check the program rules before you commit.

faqs.q: What accreditation should my solar installer hold?
faqs.a: The installer must be accredited under the federal scheme for the system to create certificates, and the person doing the electrical work must hold a current electrical licence for the state the job is in. Ask for both numbers and check them. Accreditation arrangements for solar installers have changed in recent years, so confirm the current requirement rather than accepting an old logo on a brochure.

title: What to ask before you book a country motel
description: Reception closes at 8pm in most country towns. Twelve questions on cancellation, pets, parking and after hours check in.
author: The LocalsKnow desk
body:
Country motels are not small hotels. They are usually owner operated, often with one or two staff, and the person who checks you in is frequently the person who cleaned your room. That changes what you should ask before you book, because the assumptions that hold in a city chain do not hold on the Hume.

Here is what to sort out before you pay.

## Check in, and what happens if you are late

Ask what time reception closes. In most country towns it is somewhere between 7pm and 9pm, and in the smaller ones it can be earlier if there is no restaurant.

Then ask what happens if you arrive after that. Most places have a system, usually a key safe with a code sent by text, an envelope left in a box, or a phone number that reaches the owner at home. All of that is fine. What is not fine is finding out at 10pm that there is no system.

Ring on the day if your arrival time slips. On the Hume between Melbourne and Sydney, a truck rollover can add two hours to a run, and a courtesy call is the difference between a room and a locked door.

## Cancellation, and who wrote the rule

Cancellation terms in regional accommodation are stricter than most people expect, because a small motel cannot refill a room on a Tuesday in July.

Ask three things. How far out can I cancel without a charge, what is the charge inside that window, and does a date change count as a cancellation.

The answer also depends on how you booked. A booking made through an online travel agent is governed by that platform's terms and by the rate you selected, and a non refundable rate is exactly what it says. A direct booking is governed by whatever the owner agrees, which is often more flexible, especially if you ring rather than email.

In event weeks, expect tighter terms and minimum night stays. Race meetings, field days, ute musters and football finals fill towns like Deniliquin, Wangaratta and Yarrawonga months ahead, and those bookings are often non refundable. State holidays add to it, and the two states do not share a calendar, which we set out in [the public holidays comparison](/guides/public-holidays-nsw-vs-vic/).

## Pets

Pet friendly means different things in different towns. Ask specifically.

Is the dog allowed inside the room, or only in an enclosed yard or on the verandah? Is there a fee, and is it per night or per stay? Can the dog be left alone in the room while you go to dinner? Is there a size or number limit?

Working dogs are common in country accommodation and plenty of motels will happily take a dog that stays on the ute or in a run out the back while refusing a dog inside. That is not unfriendliness, it is the cleaning bill. Get the answer before you arrive with the dog in the car.

## Parking and vehicles

Ask about the vehicle you are actually bringing. A caravan, a boat, a work trailer, a horse float or a dual cab with a tray changes the answer.

Useful questions. Is there drive up parking at the room door? Can I park a trailer without unhitching? Is there a powered spot or a place to plug in a fridge? Is the car park lit and off the street? Is there a truck bay for a large vehicle?

If you are travelling in an electric vehicle, ask whether charging is available and what type. Some regional motels have added chargers, many have not, and a standard power point at the room is often the practical answer.

## The room itself

Ground floor or upstairs matters, because most older country motels have no lift. Say so if stairs are a problem.

Ask which side the room faces. Rooms fronting the highway in towns like Holbrook, Euroa or Tarcutta hear trucks all night. Ask for a room at the back and most owners will oblige if the motel is not full.

Check the bedding configuration rather than the room name. A family room can mean a queen and two singles in one space, or two connected rooms, and those are very different if you are travelling with teenagers. Ask about heating and cooling too, because a reverse cycle unit in one room and a wall heater in another is common in older buildings.

## Food, and the country reality

Many country motels have a restaurant that opens some nights and not others. Sunday and Monday are the usual closures, and in small towns the pub may be the only alternative and may also be shut on Mondays.

Ask what is open on the night you arrive and how late. Ask whether breakfast is included, whether it is continental or cooked, and whether it needs to be ordered the night before, because in small motels it usually does.

Ask about the kettle, the toaster and the bar fridge if you plan to self cater. Kitchenettes vary wildly between rooms in the same motel.

## Booking direct or through a platform

Booking direct usually gets you a better cancellation policy, a better chance of the room you want, and the ability to negotiate a longer stay. Online travel agents get you a familiar interface, sometimes a lower headline rate, and terms that are much harder to vary.

For regional stays, a phone call is worth the two minutes. It is also the only reliable way to get the answers to everything above.

Ask about card surcharges and deposits. Many small motels take a deposit or pre authorise a card, and a surcharge on credit card payments is common and legal when it reflects the cost of acceptance.

## Twelve questions worth asking in one call

1. What time does reception close, and what is the after hours arrangement?
2. What is the cancellation window, and what does a date change cost?
3. Is the rate refundable, and does that change if I book direct?
4. Are pets allowed inside the room, and what is the fee?
5. Can I park a trailer or caravan without unhitching?
6. Is the room ground floor?
7. Is it away from the highway?
8. What is the actual bedding configuration?
9. Is breakfast included, and does it need ordering the night before?
10. Is the restaurant open on the night I arrive, and what else is open in town?
11. Is there a card surcharge or a deposit?
12. What is the checkout time, and can it be extended?

Start with the listings for [motels in Albury](/nsw/albury/motels/), [motels in Bright](/vic/bright/motels/), or the wider [motels category](/categories/motels/) and [holiday parks](/categories/holiday-parks/) if you are towing.

faqs.q: What happens if I arrive after reception closes?
faqs.a: Most country motels have an after hours system, usually a key safe with a code sent by text or an envelope left out for you. Confirm the arrangement when you book, and ring on the day if your arrival time changes. Some smaller places genuinely have no after hours option, which is exactly why you ask.

faqs.q: Are country motel cancellation policies negotiable?
faqs.a: Often yes if you booked direct and you give reasonable notice. A small motel cannot easily refill a midweek room, so goodwill goes further than a demand. Bookings made through an online travel agent are governed by that platform's terms and a non refundable rate usually stays non refundable.

faqs.q: Does pet friendly mean the dog can stay in the room?
faqs.a: Not always. Many country motels allow dogs in an enclosed yard, on a verandah or in a run, but not inside the room, and some allow it inside but not unattended. There is often a cleaning fee, charged per night or per stay. Confirm the specific arrangement before you travel with the dog.

faqs.q: Can I park a caravan or trailer at a motel?
faqs.a: Many regional motels have drive up parking that suits a trailer or a caravan, but not all, and space is tighter in town centres. Ask whether you can leave it hitched, and whether the area is lit and off the street. If you need power, ask about a powered spot or consider a holiday park instead.

faqs.q: Is it cheaper to book direct or through a booking site?
faqs.a: The headline rate is often similar, but direct booking usually gets better cancellation terms and a better chance of the specific room you want. A phone call also lets you confirm parking, pets and after hours check in in one go. For regional stays that flexibility is generally worth more than a small rate difference.

title: Starting a business in regional NSW or Victoria
description: ABN, business name, licences, insurance and workers compensation, plus why a local directory listing is worth more in a town of 8,000.
author: The LocalsKnow desk
body:
Registering a business in Australia is quick. Setting it up so it does not cause you problems in year two takes a bit longer. This is the order to do it in, and the state differences that matter if you are anywhere near the Murray.

## 1. Pick the structure before you register anything

Sole trader is the fastest and cheapest. You trade under your own name or a registered business name, you are personally liable, and the business income goes on your personal tax return.

A company is a separate legal entity registered with ASIC. It costs more to set up and carries an annual review fee, and it brings director duties and a director identification number requirement. It limits some liability, though not the liability that a director personally guarantees, and not liability for your own negligent work.

Partnerships and trusts have their place, particularly on farms and in family businesses. Talk to an accountant before you choose. Changing structure later means new registrations, new bank accounts and sometimes new licences, so the hour with the accountant is cheap.

## 2. ABN, business name and GST

Apply for an Australian Business Number through the Australian Business Register. It is free. Anyone who charges you for a plain ABN application is charging for typing.

If you trade under anything other than your own legal name, register a business name with ASIC. There is a fee, payable for one year or three years, and ASIC publishes the current amount. Registering a business name does not give you trademark rights and does not stop someone else using a similar name, so check the trade marks register too if the name matters to you.

Register for GST once your turnover reaches the registration threshold, which has sat at $75,000 for some years. Confirm the current figure with the ATO. Some businesses register earlier by choice, which lets them claim GST credits on setup costs and looks more established to commercial customers.

While you are there, sort out PAYG withholding if you will have staff, and get a business bank account. Running business money through a personal account is the single most common reason a small business has an unpleasant first tax return.

## 3. Licences and permits

This is where the state you operate in starts to matter.

Trade licences sit with NSW Fair Trading in New South Wales. In Victoria, builders and plumbers sit with the Victorian Building Authority and electrical work sits with Energy Safe Victoria. If you will work on both sides of the border, read [how a NSW licence works in Victoria](/guides/nsw-vic-licence-rules/) before you quote your first job over there, because entitlement follows the location of the work.

Food businesses register with the local council under state food law, and usually need a food safety program and a nominated food safety supervisor. Liquor is licensed by Liquor and Gaming NSW or by the Victorian liquor regulator. Mobile food vans need approval in every council area they trade in, which in border towns can mean two councils in two states.

The Australian Business Licence and Information Service is the tool for working out what applies to your activity in your location. It is free and it is more reliable than asking around.

## 4. Insurance

Public liability is the baseline. Twenty million dollars of cover is commonly required by councils, government contracts and larger commercial clients, and ten million is often the minimum anyone will accept. Get the certificate of currency and keep it where you can send it in a hurry, because clients ask for it at the worst possible time.

Beyond that, consider professional indemnity if you give advice or design, tools and plant cover, business vehicle cover that reflects commercial use, product liability if you sell goods, and business interruption.

Workers compensation is compulsory once you employ people. In New South Wales it runs through the icare scheme, and in Victoria through WorkSafe Victoria. The policy generally follows the state where the worker is based, so a business with staff on both sides of the border needs to get advice rather than guess. Sole traders and most working directors cannot cover themselves under workers compensation, which is why personal accident and income protection cover exists.

## 5. Tax and payroll obligations that differ

Income tax and GST are federal and identical in both states. Payroll tax is a state tax with different thresholds and different rates in New South Wales and Victoria, and both states adjust them. If you are approaching either threshold, check Revenue NSW and the State Revenue Office Victoria, and remember that wages can be grouped across related entities.

Land tax, stamp duty on commercial premises and vehicle registration are all state based too. On the border it is genuinely worth checking both, because the cost of the same decision can differ.

## 6. Getting found in a small market

In a town of 8,000 people, word of mouth is the strongest channel you have, and being findable is what turns word of mouth into a phone call. Someone hears your name at the footy, then searches it that night. If nothing sensible comes up, the recommendation dies there.

What actually works in regional markets:

- **Consistent details everywhere.** The same business name, address and phone number on your website, your Google Business Profile, your directory listings and your invoices. Inconsistency is what makes search engines unsure you exist.
- **A real service area.** Say which towns you cover. A Wodonga electrician who works Albury, Baranduda and Yackandandah should say so, because that is what people search.
- **Your licence number in public.** It is the fastest trust signal in the trades and most competitors leave it off. Every trade listing on this site displays the number and the date it was last checked, and buyers can verify it with the [licence check tool](/tools/licence-check/).
- **Real hours, kept current.** Being listed as open when you are shut costs you the next three calls as well.
- **Reviews asked for at the right moment.** Ask when the job is finished and the customer is happy, not a month later by email.

A directory listing does two jobs. It gets you in front of someone searching for the service in your town, and it backs up your own website with a consistent, independent record of who you are.

List your business on the category and town pages people actually use, such as [Albury](/nsw/albury/plumbers/) or [Wodonga](/vic/wodonga/electricians/), and check where your trade sits in the [category index](/categories/plumbers/) before you write your listing description.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to register a business name?
faqs.a: ASIC charges a fee for one year or three years, and the amount is indexed, so check the current figure on the ASIC website. An ABN itself is free through the Australian Business Register. Be wary of services that charge a large fee to lodge either application for you.

faqs.q: When do I have to register for GST?
faqs.a: Once your annual turnover reaches the registration threshold, which has sat at $75,000 for some years. Confirm the current figure with the ATO before you rely on it. You can register voluntarily below the threshold, which lets you claim GST credits on setup costs.

faqs.q: Do I need workers compensation as a sole trader?
faqs.a: No, and generally you cannot get it for yourself. Workers compensation covers employees, so it becomes compulsory once you hire. Sole traders and most working directors cover themselves through personal accident and income protection policies instead.

faqs.q: Which state's rules apply if I operate on both sides of the border?
faqs.a: Licensing and workplace obligations follow the location of the work and the base of the worker, not the address on your ABN record. Trade entitlement follows where the job is done, and workers compensation generally follows the state where the employee is based. Get advice before you take on staff across the border.

faqs.q: How much public liability cover do I need?
faqs.a: Ten million dollars is often the minimum a client will accept, and twenty million is commonly required by councils, government contracts and larger commercial customers. Check what your contracts specify before you buy the policy. Keep the certificate of currency handy, because clients ask for it at short notice.

faqs.q: Is a directory listing worth it for a small regional business?
faqs.a: Yes, because in a small market most enquiries start with a name someone was given and a search that follows. A listing with consistent details, real hours, a stated service area and a verifiable licence number turns that search into a call. It also strengthens the consistency signals that help your own website rank.

title: What a mobile mechanic costs out here
description: In NSW a mobile mechanic must hold a motor vehicle repairer licence. Victoria has no equivalent. Indicative border-district callout and job prices.
author: The LocalsKnow desk
body:
Most people ring a mobile mechanic for one of two reasons. The car is in the driveway and will not start, or the workshop in town has quoted three weeks and the car has to be in Wagga on Thursday. Either way the first question is the same, and almost nobody gets a straight answer to it: what will this cost, and will it cost more than simply taking the car in.

What follows is an indicative guide to mobile mechanic pricing across the border district, plus an equally important account of the jobs that cannot be done in a driveway at any price. The ranges below are indicative. They are drawn from advertised rates and from the quotes small mobile operators around Albury, Wodonga, Wagga Wagga and the Murray towns commonly give. This is not a price list, no mechanic is bound by it, and a fair quote can sit outside these ranges for good reasons. Use it as a sanity check on the number in front of you.

## How callout and hourly usually fit together

Mobile pricing tends to take one of three shapes, and the shape matters more than the headline rate.

The first is a **callout fee plus an hourly rate**. The callout covers turning up, typically somewhere between $60 and $120, and the clock starts once work begins. This is the most transparent structure and the easiest to compare against a workshop.

The second is a **minimum charge that includes the first hour**. A quoted figure of, say, $180 to $260 covers arrival and the first hour on the tools, then an hourly rate after that. Most battery, no-start and basic diagnostic jobs finish inside this window, which is why it is common.

The third is an **all-inclusive job price**, quoted for a defined piece of work such as a logbook service or a set of front pads. Travel is buried in it. This is the fairest structure for the customer when the job is predictable and the worst when it is not, because the mechanic has to price in the risk of the job going sideways.

Indicative labour rates for mobile work in the Riverina, the Murray and the north east currently sit around $110 to $160 an hour, against roughly $120 to $190 for a fixed workshop. Mobile is not automatically dearer per hour. The difference shows up in travel and in how long a job takes without a hoist.

| Job (indicative only) | Typical mobile range |
|---|---|
| Callout, on its own | $60 to $120 |
| Minimum charge including first hour | $180 to $260 |
| Hourly rate after the first hour | $110 to $160 |
| Basic logbook service, four cylinder, oil and filter | $200 to $350 |
| Battery test, supply and fit | $180 to $400 |
| Front brake pads, parts and labour | $300 to $550 |
| Front pads and discs, parts and labour | $600 to $1,100 |
| Scan and fault diagnosis, first hour | $120 to $250 |
| Pre-purchase inspection | $180 to $350 |
| After hours or weekend loading | 1.25 to 1.5 times the standard rate |

These figures are indicative ranges collected from operator advertising and customer-reported quotes in the border district during 2026. They exclude parts unless stated, and they assume a sealed, level driveway within the mechanic's normal service area.

## The travel zone is the part that decides the bill

In a metropolitan suburb the travel component of a mobile quote is noise. Out here it is often the largest single variable, because the next town is 40 kilometres away and the one after that is 60.

Nearly every operator works to a free radius, commonly 15 to 25 kilometres from their base, with travel charged beyond it. Beyond the zone the usual mechanisms are a per kilometre rate of roughly $1.10 to $2.00, or a flat surcharge of $60 to $120 per additional half hour of driving. The critical question, and the one that produces most of the disputes, is whether travel is charged one way or return. Return is the honest default. An operator based in Lavington attending a job at Culcairn, about 47 kilometres away, has driven close to 95 kilometres before parts.

Distances worth knowing when asking for a quote: Albury to Corowa is about 56 kilometres, Albury to Holbrook about 62, Wodonga to Beechworth about 40 and Wodonga to Tallangatta about 45. From Wagga Wagga it is about 40 kilometres to Junee, roughly the same to Coolamon, about 65 to Lockhart and about 85 to Temora.

Two things follow. First, ask for the base suburb, not the business address on the website, because plenty of operators run a Wodonga phone number from a Baranduda shed or vice versa. Second, ask whether the mechanic already has a run scheduled in your direction. Mobile operators batch jobs by geography, and waiting until Tuesday when they are already coming to Holbrook can remove the travel charge entirely. Nobody volunteers this. It is worth asking.

The border itself is not a travel obstacle. Crossing the Murray at Albury Wodonga costs a few minutes. The licensing consequences of crossing it are a different matter, and are covered further down.

## The jobs mobile mechanics genuinely do well

A mobile mechanic with a good van is not a lesser mechanic. There is a defined set of work where the model is simply better than a workshop.

- **Logbook servicing.** Oil, filters, fluids, a visual inspection and a stamped service book. The car is not driven anywhere, nothing sits in a queue, and the work is done in front of the owner.
- **Batteries, starters and alternators.** The most common no-start callout in the district. A battery diagnosis is more reliable done cold in the driveway than after a tow.
- **Brakes.** Pads on most vehicles, and discs on many, are straightforward on axle stands.
- **Diagnostics.** This is the underrated one. Intermittent faults often only appear on a cold start at home, which is exactly the condition a workshop cannot easily reproduce after the car has been driven in and left to idle in a bay.
- **Pre-purchase inspections.** Genuinely valuable in a district where the private sale you are considering is a Hilux on a property 60 kilometres out. Sending an independent mechanic to the vehicle is far more practical than asking a stranger to drive it to town.
- **Spark plugs, belts, hoses, coolant, filters and globes** on engines with reasonable access.

Compare listings for both models before deciding: [mobile mechanics in Albury](/nsw/albury/mobile-mechanics/), [mobile mechanics in Wodonga](/vic/wodonga/mobile-mechanics/) and [mobile mechanics in Wagga Wagga](/nsw/wagga-wagga/mobile-mechanics/) sit alongside the workshop listings under [mechanics](/categories/mechanics/).

## The jobs that need a hoist, a press or a pit

No amount of goodwill puts a driveway on equal footing with a workshop for the following, and an operator who agrees to attempt them at your house is a warning sign rather than a bargain.

- **Clutches and gearboxes.** Removing a transmission needs a hoist and a jack rated for it.
- **Wheel bearings and suspension bushes** that require a hydraulic press.
- **Coil spring work.** Compressing a road spring without proper equipment is one of the more genuinely dangerous jobs in the trade.
- **Tyre fitting, balancing and wheel alignment.** All require fixed machinery.
- **Exhaust repairs** needing welding and underbody access.
- **Air conditioning regas**, which most mobile operators do not carry.
- **Anything on soft ground.** Jack stands need a hard, level surface. A gravel or dirt driveway after rain will stop the job, and wet weather cancels more mobile bookings than anything else.

There is also the waste question. Used oil, coolant and brake fluid have to leave the property with the mechanic. Ask what happens to them. A professional operator will answer without hesitating.

Two things that are frequently assumed and are simply not available mobile: a NSW pink slip and a Victorian roadworthy certificate. Both require an inspection authority tied to premises, not a person, and no mobile mechanic can issue either from a driveway.

## Where the rules differ

This is the part that surprises people who move across the river. The two states treat repair work completely differently.

| | NSW | VIC |
|---|---|---|
| Licence to run a repair business | Motor vehicle repairer licence required. NSW Fair Trading states this applies if you "run a mobile repair business" | No equivalent repairer licence. The Victorian motor car trader's licence covers buying, selling and exchanging cars, not repairing them |
| Individual credential | Motor vehicle tradesperson certificate, in each class of work performed, across 16 classes including motor mechanic and automotive electrician | No state certificate. Trade qualification and association membership are the only markers |
| Public register to check | Free licence check through Service NSW by name, licence number, ABN or postcode | No repairer register. The public register covers motor car traders only |
| Licence cost to the operator | New licence $914 for one year, $1,304 for three, $2,390 for five, with a discount for applying online. Renewal from $285 | Not applicable |
| Rego safety inspection | eSafety check, or pink slip, for most light vehicles over five years old, only at an Authorised Inspection Scheme station, valid six months | No annual roadworthy for registration renewal |
| Selling a registered car | Not required for a private sale | Certificate of roadworthiness less than 30 days old, issued by a licensed vehicle tester |

The NSW licence fees above are current as at August 2026, took effect on 1 July 2026, and NSW Fair Trading notes fees may increase in line with CPI at the start of each financial year. The maximum a NSW inspection station may charge for a light vehicle safety check is $52 including GST, also effective 1 July 2026.

NSW exempts minor work that does not affect the mechanical operation or structure of a vehicle or any vehicle safety feature. That exemption is narrower than it sounds. Brakes, steering and suspension are all inside the licensing net.

The border consequence is worth spelling out. The NSW requirement attaches to carrying on repair work in NSW, including mobile work. A Wodonga-based operator who regularly services cars in Albury, Lavington and Thurgoona should be able to say without hesitation how they are covered, and their licence should appear on the Service NSW check. Ask the question and run the check. It takes under a minute and it is free. In Victoria there is nothing to check, so the substitutes are a current trade qualification, public liability insurance, an ABN, and membership of RACV or VACC, which Consumer Affairs Victoria itself points consumers toward.

NSW licensees also have obligations most customers never see, including a parts register recording where components came from. NSW Fair Trading's guidance puts penalties of up to $5,500 on failing to keep that register properly. It is one reason a licensed operator's paperwork tends to be better.

## What happens to the money when the job turns into a workshop job

This is the scenario the brochures skip. The mechanic arrives, spends 40 minutes diagnosing, and concludes the car needs a hoist.

That diagnostic time is legitimately payable. The mechanic drove out and did skilled work, and the answer, even though it is not the answer anyone wanted, has value. The question is not whether you pay but what you agreed to pay, and that must be settled on the phone before the booking, not in the driveway afterwards.

Ask these three things in advance:

1. If the fault turns out to need a workshop, what is the charge for the visit, and is it the callout only, the diagnostic time only, or both.
2. Does that amount come off the bill if the job goes to a workshop the mechanic is connected to, or if they tow it in themselves. Some operators run a shed as well as a van and will credit it. Many will not, and that is not unreasonable, but it should be known.
3. Who arranges and pays for the tow. Towing within a town in this district commonly runs $150 to $300 indicatively, and considerably more between towns.

Consumer Affairs Victoria advises getting a written estimate before any work is done, covering the work to be done, parts to be supplied, estimated time of completion, estimated parts and labour costs and the method of payment, and making it clear the mechanic must call before commencing any repair that has not been authorised. That advice is sound on both sides of the river. A text message confirming the estimate is a written estimate.

Underneath all of this sits the Australian Consumer Law, which applies identically in both states. Services must be provided with due care and skill, be fit for the stated purpose, and be supplied within a reasonable time. Where the failure is minor, the business must fix it at no cost. Where it is major, including where the work has created an unsafe situation, the customer can cancel and seek a refund, which may be reduced for work already completed, or keep the contract and seek compensation for the drop in value. A mobile mechanic is bound by this exactly as a workshop is.

## Comparing a mobile quote with a workshop quote fairly

Comparing hourly rates alone will mislead, in both directions.

**Add your own travel to the workshop quote.** A workshop job means two trips, drop off and collect. From Corowa to Albury that is roughly 220 kilometres of driving before anyone touches the car, plus the fuel and most of a day. Regional workshops rarely offer courtesy cars.

**Add the time cost.** A day off the farm or off a shift is a real number. Put it in.

**Check GST.** A sole operator with GST turnover under $75,000 is not required to register for GST, so their price contains none. A larger workshop's price does. Two quotes of $400 are not the same quote if only one carries an input tax credit you can claim on a business vehicle.

**Ask who supplies the parts and who warrants them.** Mobile operators often source aftermarket parts or ask the customer to supply them. A part you supply is a part nobody else warrants, and the labour to fit it a second time is yours.

**Ask about labour warranty in months, not adjectives.** Get the answer in writing.

**Compare the total, not the rate.** A workshop at $170 an hour that does a brake job in 1.5 hours on a hoist beats a mobile at $130 an hour taking three hours on a driveway. The reverse is true for a battery.

## Before the mechanic arrives

Clear the driveway and park the car on hard, level ground with room on both sides. Do not have it boxed in behind another vehicle. Find the wheel lock key, which lives in the glovebox or under the boot floor and is the single most common reason a brake or tyre job gets abandoned on arrival. Have the logbook out, along with any receipts for recent work. Note down when the fault happens rather than just what it does, because cold, hot, wet and after a long drive are four different faults. If the car has been sitting for weeks, say so when booking.

Then ask for the estimate in writing before anyone lifts a bonnet, and in NSW, run the licence check. It is the cheapest 60 seconds in the whole transaction.

faqs.q: Does a mobile mechanic need a licence in NSW?
faqs.a: Yes. NSW Fair Trading states that a motor vehicle repairer licence is required if you own a repair business, work as a self-employed repairer or run a mobile repair business. Individuals must also hold a motor vehicle tradesperson certificate in each class of repair work they perform, across 16 classes including motor mechanic and automotive electrician. Minor work that does not affect a vehicle's mechanical operation, structure or safety features is exempt. Licences can be checked free through Service NSW.

faqs.q: Does a mobile mechanic need a licence in Victoria?
faqs.a: No. Victoria has no occupational licence for motor vehicle repairers. The Victorian motor car trader's licence covers buying, selling and exchanging motor cars, generally where four or more cars are traded a year, and does not extend to repair work. Because there is no register to check, Consumer Affairs Victoria points consumers toward mechanics affiliated with RACV or VACC. Trade qualification, public liability insurance and an ABN are the practical substitutes for a licence check.

faqs.q: Can a mobile mechanic do a pink slip or a roadworthy certificate?
faqs.a: No. In NSW only an Authorised Inspection Scheme station can perform an eSafety check, commonly called a pink slip, which most light vehicles more than five years old need annually and which is valid for six months. The maximum fee for a light vehicle check is $52 including GST as at August 2026. In Victoria a certificate of roadworthiness must be issued by a licensed vehicle tester and be less than 30 days old when a registered vehicle is sold.

faqs.q: What does a mobile mechanic charge for a callout around Albury Wodonga and Wagga?
faqs.a: Indicatively, a standalone callout runs $60 to $120, or $180 to $260 for a minimum charge covering arrival plus the first hour, with $110 to $160 an hour after that. These ranges come from operator advertising and customer-reported quotes across the border district in 2026 and are not a price list. Travel beyond a free radius of roughly 15 to 25 kilometres is usually charged at about $1.10 to $2.00 per kilometre, often calculated return.

faqs.q: Do I still pay if the mechanic decides the job needs a workshop?
faqs.a: Usually yes. The diagnostic time and the travel are real work and are legitimately chargeable. What varies is the amount and whether it is credited later. Settle it before booking by asking three questions: what is charged if the job cannot be completed on site, does that amount come off a subsequent workshop bill, and who arranges and pays for any tow. Get the answer by text so it is in writing.

faqs.q: Which jobs cannot be done in a driveway?
faqs.a: Anything needing a hoist, a hydraulic press or fixed machinery. That means clutches and gearboxes, pressed wheel bearings and suspension bushes, coil spring work, tyre fitting, balancing, wheel alignment and exhaust welding. Air conditioning regas is rarely offered mobile. Work also cannot proceed safely on soft or sloping ground, so a gravel driveway after rain will stop the job. Neither a NSW pink slip nor a Victorian roadworthy certificate can be issued mobile.

faqs.q: How do I compare a mobile quote against a workshop quote fairly?
faqs.a: Compare totals, not hourly rates. Add two return trips and a lost half day to the workshop quote, which from Corowa to Albury is roughly 220 kilometres. Check GST, because an operator with turnover under $75,000 is not required to register and their price contains none. Ask who supplies and warrants the parts, and ask for the labour warranty in months. A hoist can halve the hours on some jobs and is irrelevant on others.

faqs.q: What are my rights if the mobile repair does not fix the problem?
faqs.a: The Australian Consumer Law applies identically in NSW and Victoria. Services must be supplied with due care and skill, be fit for the stated purpose and be delivered within a reasonable time. For a minor failure the business must fix the problem at no cost. For a major failure, including work that creates an unsafe situation, you can cancel and seek a refund, potentially reduced for work completed, or keep the contract and seek compensation for the reduced value.

title: Buying second-hand car parts
description: NSW wreckers must mark every prescribed part with its register entry number and keep the record six years. What that means when you buy used parts.
author: The LocalsKnow desk
body:
The dealership has quoted a number that is a decent fraction of what the car is worth, the insurer is not involved, and somebody at work has said to ring a wrecker. That is where most people start, and it is the point where the wrong question gets asked first. The question is not who is cheapest. It is whether this particular part should ever be bought used at all, and if it should, what has to be said on the phone so the right one turns up the first time.

What follows describes how the used parts trade actually works across the Murray, where a yard in [Wodonga](/vic/wodonga/wreckers/) and a yard in [Albury](/nsw/albury/wreckers/) sit ten minutes apart and keep their records under two different state schemes. It is general information rather than legal advice, and no yard is bound by any of it.

## What is worth buying used

Recyclers exist because the parts that break most often are the parts nobody stocks new for a fifteen year old vehicle. The items that reliably justify a used purchase are the ones where condition can be judged by looking at them.

- Body panels and closures. Doors, bonnets, guards, tailgates, bumper bars and hatches. Colour matching is a bonus rather than a plan, because a blend is common anyway.
- Lamp assemblies, mirrors, grilles, badges and the trim clips that snap the moment anyone touches them.
- Interior parts. Seats, door cards, dash sections, switches, sun visors and centre consoles.
- Door and quarter glass. Windscreens generally come from a glazier rather than a yard.
- Engines, gearboxes, transfer cases and differentials. The largest saving and the largest exposure, so these are the items where a written warranty matters most.
- Ancillaries such as alternators, starters, power steering pumps, air conditioning compressors and turbochargers, though a reconditioned unit is often the better buy.
- Electronic modules. Engine computers, body control modules, clusters and head units, subject to whether the module is coded to the vehicle identification number.
- Wheels, subframes, control arms, knuckles and hubs.

## What to never buy used, and why

The test is simple. If the property that determines whether the part is safe cannot be seen, measured or documented, do not buy it second hand.

- **Airbags and airbag control modules.** Nobody can look at an inflator and tell whether the propellant has degraded, whether the unit has already fired and been reset, or whether it belongs to a recall. Consumer Affairs Victoria states plainly that any second-hand airbag used must be one that has not been activated previously. The compulsory Takata recall was issued on 27 February 2018 and covered more than three million vehicles, and suppliers of vehicles or parts carry ongoing obligations under it. A salvaged inflator of unknown history can quietly be a recalled one.
- **Seatbelts, retractors and pretensioners.** A belt that has taken a load stretches and a pretensioner that has fired is spent. Neither shows on inspection, and both matter only once.
- **Brake friction material.** Pads and shoes are inexpensive new, and contamination or glazing is invisible until the pedal goes long.
- **Timing belts, tensioners, idlers and water pumps.** The part is cheap and the labour is not. A used timing component saves perhaps a tenth of the job and risks the whole engine.
- **Rubber and anything that carries fluid.** Hoses, brake lines, engine mounts, constant velocity boots and drive belts age on the shelf regardless of kilometres travelled.
- **Filters, plugs, wiper blades and batteries.** The saving is trivial and the failure is guaranteed.

Structural sections cut from a crashed shell without documentation belong on the same list. If a yard cannot say which vehicle a section came from, that is the answer.

## How interchange works, and why a part from a different year fits

Manufacturers do not build a new door for every model year. One pressing serves several years, several trim levels, sometimes two body styles and occasionally two badges where a platform was shared. A facelift usually changes the parts a customer sees, such as lamps, grille and bumper, and leaves the hidden structure alone. That is why a yard will confidently offer a 2014 door for a 2011 car and be right.

Yards resolve this through interchange tables built into their inventory software, descended from the Hollander interchange system that grouped functionally identical part numbers long before any of it went online. When a counter hand asks for the build date instead of the year, that is the interchange lookup talking.

The traps are consistent:

- **Running changes.** Manufacturers alter parts mid model year, so the month and year on the build plate settle arguments the registration papers cannot.
- **Market of delivery.** An Australian delivered vehicle and an imported example of the same model can differ in lighting, wiring and mounting points.
- **Connectors.** The casting can be identical and the plug three pins different.
- **Coding.** Many modules are married to a vehicle identification number and need a scan tool before they will function. Ask before buying, not after fitting.
- **Handedness and body style.** Left and right, sedan and wagon, cab chassis and ute tub.

## What to tell the yard so you are not sold the wrong part twice

The information below is what a counter hand needs to run the interchange properly. Volunteering it unprompted saves the second trip.

1. The vehicle identification number, seventeen characters, from the build plate, the base of the windscreen, the driver's door jamb or the registration papers.
2. The build date, month and year, from the build plate. This is not the same as the year on the papers, and on imports it is not the compliance date either.
3. The engine code and engine number.
4. The transmission code, plus automatic or manual and two wheel or all wheel drive.
5. The paint code and trim code, both usually on the build plate, for anything that has to match.
6. The part number cast or stamped on the old part, photographed. This is the strongest identifier available and it outranks every description.
7. Photographs of the part in place, both sides, including the electrical connector.

Ask one more question at the point of sale. In New South Wales, prescribed parts must be marked with the entry number from the yard's parts register. In Victoria, the dealer's identification number must stay affixed to the item until it is sold. Ask for that number on the invoice. It is the cheapest traceability available and it costs the yard nothing to provide.

## The networks that search other yards

A yard that does not have the part on its own shelves does not simply say no. It broadcasts the request to a network of other yards, which reply with what they hold, the grade, the kilometres and a freight price. Parts Search Australia and Auto Parts Bridge are the two systems most commonly used for this in Australia, alongside group and association networks that member yards run among themselves.

Panels are usually graded by damage, along the lines of A for straight, B for minor dents and scratches, C for repairable. Drivetrain is listed with kilometres and with whether it was tested or pulled from a stationary vehicle. Neither grading system is standardised across the industry, so ask what the grade means at that particular yard.

For anyone on this border, the useful part is that the broadcast does not stop at the river. A request taken in [Wagga Wagga](/nsw/wagga-wagga/wreckers/) reaches yards in [Wangaratta](/vic/wangaratta/wreckers/) and [Shepparton](/vic/shepparton/wreckers/) the same way it reaches Griffith or Cootamundra. What does change at the river is which licensing scheme governs the yard holding the part, and what it had to write down when the part came off the vehicle.

## What warranty a used part actually carries

Buying from a business, in either state, brings the Australian Consumer Law with it. The consumer guarantees cover acceptable quality, fitness for a stated purpose and matching the description. Acceptable quality is judged against age and against how long similar products normally last, so a twelve year old cylinder head is not held to the standard of a new one, but it still has to be a working cylinder head.

Buying privately is a different transaction. The ACCC's position on second-hand cars is that most consumer guarantees and state and territory laws do not apply to purchases through private or auction sales, and the same reasoning follows the part. A gearbox bought off a marketplace listing or out of a shed at a swap meet carries whatever the seller promised and nothing else.

Where a yard offers something extra, such as three months on a panel or twelve months on an engine, that promise is a warranty against defects under the ACL, and the written document has requirements. The ACCC lists them: the business name, address, email and telephone number, what the consumer has to do to claim, how to make the claim, what the business will do about it, how long the warranty runs, who bears the expenses and how they are recovered, a statement that the benefits are in addition to other legal rights, and prescribed mandatory text. That document has to be physically available with the product. A sign on the wall or a page on a website does not satisfy it.

So ask for it on paper, and ask it to state five things: the duration in months and kilometres, whether it covers the part only or the part and the labour to refit it, who pays freight on a warranty return, whether a core charge applies to the old unit, and what voids it. Then keep the invoice with the donor vehicle identification number and the register or identification number on it.

## Where the rules differ

The Australian Consumer Law is national. Everything behind the counter is not.

| Question | New South Wales | Victoria |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Licence to dismantle vehicles and sell parts | A motor vehicle recycler licence from NSW Fair Trading, covering buying, dismantling and selling major body and mechanical components or prescribed parts. Operating unlicensed draws a $5,500 penalty notice, or prosecution to a maximum of $110,000 for a first offence. A one year licence applied for online costs $665 from 1 July 2026. | Auto wreckers and recyclers who buy car parts must register as second-hand dealers. A motor car trader's licence is also required to buy vehicles from the public in order to dismantle them, with exemptions for yards that buy only written-off, incomplete or damaged vehicles, or that exclusively buy and sell parts. |
| Record of each individual part | A parts register, Form 3, with the entry made within one business day and records kept six years. Twenty prescribed parts are covered, including airbags, engines, transmissions, doors, bonnets, boot lids, wheels and headlights. Failing to keep records draws a $550 penalty notice or prosecution to a maximum of $2,200. | A bound record book or computerised system recording the description and identifying marks, a dealer assigned identification number, the seller's name, address and identification, the date and time of receipt, the price paid and the employee's name. Lots where each item is worth under $100 may be entered as a single line. |
| Marking on the part itself | Prescribed parts must be clearly marked with the matching register entry number, in indelible ink or on a durable label. | The dealer's identification number must remain affixed to the item until it is sold. |
| Second-hand airbags | Airbags are one of the twenty prescribed parts, so each one must be registered and marked. | Consumer Affairs Victoria states that any second-hand airbag used must be one that has not been activated previously. |
| Consumer guarantees on the part | Australian Consumer Law, applying when the seller is a business and not to private sales. | Identical. The law does not change at the bridge. |

Two further differences are worth knowing before the part gets fitted. New South Wales licenses motor vehicle repair businesses and requires a motor vehicle tradesperson certificate for the people doing the work, with an exemption for minor repairs that do not affect mechanical operation, structure or safety features. Consumer Affairs Victoria's guidance for choosing a workshop points instead to getting a written estimate before work starts, making clear that no unauthorised work is to begin, and choosing a mechanic who belongs to an industry association bound by a code of conduct. Victorian guidance also confirms something useful anywhere: the mechanic must give you the parts removed from your car if you ask for them, other than parts that have to go back to a manufacturer for a warranty claim. Ask for the old part. It is the only way to confirm what was actually replaced.

Anyone buying a whole vehicle to strip should check it against the written-off vehicles register first. Transport for NSW publishes a searchable register at wovr.transport.nsw.gov.au, and approval to repair and re-register a written-off light vehicle is available only in very limited circumstances. A donor that will never see a plate again is fine. A donor bought in the belief it can be registered is often not.

## Used, reconditioned or aftermarket on the big items

On anything expensive, the decision has three doors rather than two.

| Item | Used from a yard | Reconditioned | New aftermarket |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Engine | Common. Ask for kilometres, compression figures and the donor identification number | Available as a short or long block, longer warranty, core charge applies | Rarely economic outside performance work |
| Automatic transmission | Common, but the failure mode is invisible on a shelf | Preferred by many workshops purely for the warranty | Limited supply for older models |
| Turbocharger | Possible, though shaft play tells you little about the next 50,000 km | Usually the better buy, balanced and re-cored | Available for common applications |
| Alternator or starter | Quick and inexpensive | Good value where a core charge applies | Often the cheapest of the three |
| Body panel | Usually the only sensible option | Not applicable | Fit and finish vary widely between suppliers |
| Headlight assembly | Check for lens crazing and internal moisture | Restoration services exist for lenses | Check mounting tabs and beam pattern before paying |

On price, the pattern recyclers in the Riverina and north east Victoria commonly describe is a used panel at roughly a third to a half of the genuine new part, a used engine or gearbox at roughly a quarter to a half of a reconditioned unit, and a reconditioned unit carrying two to three times the warranty period of the used one. Those are indicative ranges drawn from what small yards in the region quote, offered as a sanity check on the number in front of you. They are not a price list and no yard is bound by them.

## Freight or drive

Distance is the part of this that the border makes odd. Albury to Wodonga is a few minutes. Wangaratta is about 75 km from Albury, Wagga Wagga about 130 km, Shepparton about 190 km, Melbourne about 320 km from Wodonga and Sydney about 550 km from Albury. A part that would be a freight decision in most of the country is a lunchtime errand here.

- **Panels and closures.** These travel badly. Ask whether the item will be blanket wrapped or crated, what the crating costs, and who wears a damage claim if it arrives with a new dent. For anything inside a two hour drive, going to get it is usually cheaper and always more certain.
- **Engines and gearboxes.** Pallet freight, with a forklift needed at both ends. Confirm the yard can load it and work out how it comes off the tray before the truck arrives.
- **Glass and mirrors.** High breakage rates. Source locally where possible.
- **Modules, switches and small hard parts.** Post them. This is where freight makes obvious sense.

Driving has one advantage that no freight quote captures. You can look at the part before money changes hands, hold the old one against it, and walk away. Take the old part with you. Many yards along the Hume corridor consolidate deliveries in each direction, so it is worth asking when the next run is going your way before paying for a dedicated freight movement.

## Before you ring the first yard

Photograph three things: the build plate, the part number on the old part, and the part still in place with its connector visible. Write down the paint code if a panel is involved. Decide, before anyone quotes you, the furthest you are willing to drive, because that number decides whether a freight price is worth arguing about.

Then ask whoever answers the phone three questions. How long is the warranty and does it cover the labour to refit. What is the register entry or identification number marked on the part. Can that warranty come through as a document with the invoice rather than as a verbal assurance. A yard that answers all three without hesitating has its paperwork in order, and a yard whose paperwork is in order is generally a yard whose parts are too.

Related: [wreckers and dismantlers](/categories/wreckers/), [auto parts suppliers](/categories/auto-parts/), and [mechanics in Albury](/nsw/albury/mechanics/) and [Wodonga](/vic/wodonga/mechanics/).

## Sources

Checked on 2026-08-25. Government fees and rules are indexed and revised, so open the source before you rely on a figure.

- [accc.gov.au](https://www.accc.gov.au/consumers/buying-products-and-services/consumer-guarantees)
- [productsafety.gov.au](https://www.productsafety.gov.au/recalls/compulsory-takata-airbag-recall)
- [nsw.gov.au](https://www.nsw.gov.au/business-and-economy/running-a-business/industry-specific-business-requirements/working-as-a-motor-vehicle-recycler)
- [consumer.vic.gov.au](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/licensing-and-registration/second-hand-dealers-and-pawnbrokers/registration/trading-in-cars-and-car-parts)

faqs.q: Is it legal to buy and fit a second-hand airbag in NSW or Victoria?
faqs.a: Consumer Affairs Victoria states that any second-hand airbag used must be one that has not been activated previously. In New South Wales airbags are one of the twenty prescribed parts a licensed recycler must enter in its parts register and mark with the entry number. Beyond that, the compulsory Takata recall issued on 27 February 2018 covers more than three million vehicles and imposes ongoing obligations on suppliers of vehicles and parts. Buy airbags new.

faqs.q: What warranty comes with a used part bought from a wrecking yard?
faqs.a: Buying from a business brings the Australian Consumer Law guarantees, including acceptable quality judged against the part's age and what similar products normally do. Any extra promise, such as three months on a panel, is a warranty against defects and the ACCC requires the written document to state the business details, how to claim, what the business will do, the duration, who pays expenses, and prescribed mandatory text. It must be supplied physically with the part.

faqs.q: Do consumer guarantees apply if I buy a part privately or at auction?
faqs.a: Generally no. The ACCC's position on second-hand cars is that most consumer guarantees and state and territory laws do not apply to purchases made through private or auction sales, and the same reasoning follows an individual part. A gearbox bought from a marketplace listing, a shed or a swap meet carries only what the seller expressly promised. Buying from a licensed yard costs more and buys a remedy.

faqs.q: Why does a wrecker ask for my build date instead of the model year?
faqs.a: Manufacturers make running changes partway through a model year, so two cars sold as the same year can take different parts. The build plate carries the month and year the vehicle was actually assembled, which is what the yard's interchange software uses to group functionally identical part numbers. The registration papers show a different date entirely, and on imported vehicles the compliance date is different again.

faqs.q: How do wreckers find a part they do not have in stock?
faqs.a: They broadcast the request to a national network of other yards, which reply with what they hold, its condition grade, the kilometres on it and a freight price. Parts Search Australia and Auto Parts Bridge are the systems most commonly used, alongside association and group networks. The search crosses the state line freely, so a request taken in Albury routinely returns stock held in Wangaratta or Shepparton.

faqs.q: What information should I give the yard to avoid being sold the wrong part?
faqs.a: Give the seventeen character vehicle identification number, the build date from the build plate, the engine code and number, the transmission code, whether the vehicle is two or all wheel drive, and the paint and trim codes for anything that has to match. Then photograph the part number stamped on the old part. That number is the strongest identifier available and it settles disputes that descriptions cannot.

faqs.q: Should I buy a used gearbox or a reconditioned one?
faqs.a: A used automatic transmission is cheaper but its failure mode is invisible on a shelf, so the purchase rests entirely on the warranty. A reconditioned unit is rebuilt to a specification, usually carries a longer written warranty, and typically involves a core charge refunded when the old unit is returned. Given that the labour cost is identical either way, most workshops recommend the reconditioned unit for exactly that reason.

faqs.q: Can a wrecker sell parts from a written-off vehicle?
faqs.a: Yes, dismantling written-off vehicles for parts is core recycler business, and in New South Wales a motor vehicle recycler licence specifically covers written-off light vehicles registered here or interstate. What is restricted is putting the vehicle back on the road. Transport for NSW publishes a searchable written-off vehicles register, and approval to repair and re-register a written-off light vehicle is granted only in very limited circumstances.

title: Moving car registration across the border
description: A Victorian car always needs a NSW blue slip; a NSW car moving to Victoria usually needs no roadworthy at all. What the border actually costs.
author: The LocalsKnow desk
body:
Nobody moves house and thinks about the car. It sits in the driveway at the new place in Wodonga with New South Wales plates still on it, and a fortnight later somebody at work mentions you were meant to do something about that. It happens the other way too. You buy a ute from a yard on Melbourne Road, drive it home to Lavington, and find the registration you assumed came with it stopped being any use the moment you crossed the bridge.

What follows is what each state actually requires when a vehicle crosses the Murray for good. Every rule here was checked against Service NSW, Transport for NSW, VicRoads, Revenue NSW, the State Revenue Office Victoria, SIRA and the Transport Accident Commission in August 2026. Fees, duty thresholds and TAC charges in both states are indexed and most moved on 1 July 2026, so treat every figure as current at that date and no further.

## The asymmetry that explains almost everything

The two states do not treat an incoming vehicle the same way, and once that lands the rest makes sense.

Victoria takes a New South Wales car largely on trust. VicRoads does not require a Certificate of Roadworthiness if the interstate registration is current, or expired less than three months before the day of your appointment, and the vehicle is going into the same name it was already registered in. The vehicle must not have been modified, and it must now be garaged in Victoria.

New South Wales inspects every time. Transport for NSW lists "has been brought into NSW from another state or territory" as a circumstance that requires an Authorised Unregistered Vehicle Inspection Scheme report, better known as a blue slip. Current Victorian registration does not change that.

So the Albury household moving to Wodonga books an appointment and hands over the plates. The Wodonga household moving to Albury books an inspection first, then queues at Service NSW with a folder of paper. Same river, very different afternoon.

## Taking your own car from Albury to Wodonga

You cannot do this online. VicRoads requires an appointment in person at a Customer Service Centre.

Bring the New South Wales plates, which are surrendered on the spot, a completed vehicle registration form, and evidence of identity including your Victorian garage address if it differs from your residential address. At the counter VicRoads checks the documents, takes the plates and gives you a receipt, takes payment for registration and TAC charges, and issues Victorian plates. Bring a screwdriver. The new plates must be on before you drive away, and the car park is where most people learn this.

You do not pay motor vehicle duty. VicRoads says so plainly on its own page, and the State Revenue Office confirms the exemption applies when a person registers a vehicle in Victoria in the same name as its previous interstate registration.

The three month figure is the one to diarise. If your New South Wales registration lapsed more than three months before your appointment date, the waiver is gone and you need a Victorian roadworthy from a licensed vehicle tester. Book the VicRoads appointment while the New South Wales rego is still alive, not after it dies.

## Taking your own car from Wodonga to Albury

Start with the blue slip. An Authorised Unregistered Vehicle Inspection Scheme report is required and there is no talking your way out of it. The maximum fee for a light vehicle is $82 including GST, and $51 for a motorcycle, effective 1 July 2026. The report is valid for 42 days, so there is no advantage in getting it early. Find an accredited station on the New South Wales side through [vehicle inspection providers in Albury](/nsw/albury/vehicle-inspections/).

Then buy a compulsory third party green slip. You cannot register without one, and you buy it yourself from a licensed insurer before you go near Service NSW.

Then lodge the lot: the Application for Registration form, proof of identity, proof of registration entitlement, the original hard copy of the blue slip, your CTP, and the original Victorian number plates. Claim the stamp duty exemption by producing your current Victorian certificate of registration in your name. Revenue NSW exempts a vehicle registered in your name in another state or territory on which you have already paid duty.

If the car is unregistered when you need to drive it to the inspection, apply for an unregistered vehicle permit. It covers one journey by the most direct route and, in Service NSW's words, "cannot be used as a substitute for full registration".

## Where the rules differ

| | Registering in New South Wales | Registering in Victoria |
|---|---|---|
| Your own car, rego current | Blue slip required regardless | No roadworthy required |
| Your own car, rego lapsed | Blue slip required regardless | No roadworthy if lapsed under 3 months |
| Car bought across the border | Blue slip required | Victorian roadworthy from a licensed tester |
| Inspection fee | Capped at $82 for a light vehicle | Not price regulated |
| Injury insurance | CTP green slip, bought separately before registering | TAC charge, billed inside the registration |
| What sets that premium | Insurer's own rating, including your demerit points | Vehicle class and postcode risk zone only |
| Duty on moving your own car | Exempt, produce the interstate certificate | Exempt, same name as the previous registration |
| New plates | $58 | $44.20 for a pair |
| Booking | Walk in to a Service NSW centre | Appointment only, in person |

## The green slip and the TAC charge are not the same thing

This is the difference that costs people the most and is understood the least.

In New South Wales, compulsory third party cover is a separate product. You shop for it. SIRA regulates the scheme but insurers set their own prices, adjusting the premium on rating factors that include your age, driving history, demerit points, claims history, the age of the vehicle, whether you hold comprehensive cover and where the car is parked. Demerit points from the past three years and four months can lift the price even if the points themselves have since been removed. The total always includes GST and the Fund Levy, which averaged $190.60 across all policyholders from 15 January 2026, up from $164.80 the year before.

In Victoria there is nothing to shop for. The Transport Accident Commission charge arrives inside the registration bill, and it is set by two things only: the class of vehicle and the postcode where it is garaged. Your driving record is irrelevant to it.

Postcodes matter, and Wodonga does well out of them. The 2026 schedule lists the high risk and medium risk postcodes and states that Victorian postcodes not listed are deemed low risk. No postcode in the 3600s appears on either list. For a sedan, station wagon or 4WD passenger vehicle in the low risk zone, the annual TAC charge is $429.00, plus $39.00 GST and $42.90 duty, for a total of $471.90. The same car garaged in metropolitan Melbourne pays $606.10. Pensioners get 50 per cent off the TAC charge, eligible apprentices pay none of it, and the charge is indexed to CPI every 1 July.

A driver carrying demerit points who moves from Albury to Wodonga can watch their injury premium fall for reasons that have nothing to do with them. Moving the other way, the same record starts costing money again.

## What a year costs on each side

The two states measure vehicles differently, New South Wales by tare weight and Victoria by body type and carrying capacity, so what follows compares bills rather than like for like categories.

| Annual cost, ordinary family car | Albury | Wodonga |
|---|---|---|
| Registration fee | $84 | included |
| Vehicle tax or registration charge | $391 (private, 1,151 to 1,500 kg tare) | included |
| Injury insurance | green slip, priced by your insurer | included |
| Knowable before you start | $475 plus a green slip | $824.60 |

For the two to land in the same place, that Albury green slip would need to come in at roughly $350. Whether it does depends entirely on who is driving.

The gap widens for work vehicles. A private ute or van in the 1,501 to 2,500 kg tare band pays $596 in New South Wales motor vehicle tax, and $924 if it is used for business, before the green slip. In Victoria, a ute, tray or van up to two tonnes in the rural low risk zone is $676.70 for the year, TAC included. Tradespeople working both sides of the river out of [Wodonga](/vic/wodonga/) and [Albury](/nsw/albury/) tend to find this out when the first renewal lands.

> Registration follows where the vehicle is garaged, not where you collect your post. Victoria's duty exemption is conditional on the Commissioner being satisfied the interstate registration was not made to avoid Victorian duty. A border postcode of convenience is not a plan.

## Duty only bites when you buy

Nobody pays stamp duty twice for moving. Both states exempt a vehicle coming across in the same name. Duty applies when ownership changes, which is where buying across the river gets interesting.

New South Wales charges $3 for every $100 of value up to $44,999. From $45,000 it is published as $1,350 plus $5 for every $100. The $1,350 is exactly the duty on the first $45,000 at the lower rate, so the $5 applies to the value above it. Use the Revenue NSW calculator rather than working it out in your head.

Victoria charges by the $200. From 1 July 2026, an ordinary passenger car up to $80,809 is $8.40 per $200 or part thereof, rising to $10.40 to $100,000, $14.00 to $150,000 and $18.00 above that. A green passenger car, meaning combined tailpipe emissions of 120 grams of carbon dioxide per kilometre or less, stays at $8.40 at any value. New non-passenger vehicles, a category that includes utes, dual cabs and motorcycles, are $5.40 per $200, but a used one being transferred goes back to $8.40.

On a $30,000 used sedan that is $900 of duty in New South Wales against $1,260 in Victoria. On a $50,000 one it is $1,600 against $2,100. Duty is only part of the sum, and a better car at a [Wodonga dealer](/vic/wodonga/car-dealers/) can still beat a worse one in [Albury](/nsw/albury/car-dealers/), but the difference is real money and belongs in the sums.

Buying a car interstate and bringing it into Victoria is a different transaction from moving your own. VicRoads requires a roadworthy from a Victorian licensed vehicle tester in that case, because the vehicle is not yet registered in your name.

## What happens to the rego you are leaving behind

Registering in the new state does not necessarily cancel the old one. VicRoads warns of exactly this. You have to go and end it yourself.

Leaving New South Wales, you lodge a refund request with Service NSW using form 1565, with the interstate surrendered plate receipt or the New South Wales plates, proof of identity and your new interstate certificate of registration. Only the motor vehicle tax comes back. The registration fee and the plate fee do not. Allow six to eight weeks.

Leaving Victoria, you cancel through myVicRoads and request the refund on the same form. The refund covers the time left on your registration, less a $22.10 processing fee and 10 per cent of the TAC charge. If the remainder is smaller than those deductions you get nothing. Payment lands within ten business days.

The green slip is the one that catches people. SIRA's published eligibility for a partial CTP refund covers vehicles that have been written off, taken to an auto wrecker, or stolen. A move interstate is not on that list, and a sold vehicle is expressly excluded because the policy attaches to the car rather than the owner. Ring your insurer before assuming anything, and if you have any choice about timing, moving to Victoria near the end of your green slip year is worth real money.

## The pink slip rule that catches border towns

Once you are registered in New South Wales and living in Albury, your annual safety inspection has to happen in New South Wales. Transport for NSW will accept an interstate inspection report only if you are more than 50 kilometres from the New South Wales border.

Read that again if you live in Albury, Corowa, Mulwala, Tocumwal or Moama. The concession exists for people genuinely distant from the state, which means it is precisely the border towns that cannot use it. The workshop three minutes away in Wodonga may have serviced the car for a decade. Its roadworthy certificate will not renew your pink slip. A [Wagga Wagga](/nsw/wagga-wagga/vehicle-inspections/) driver stranded in Victoria has options here. An Albury one does not.

Victoria is simpler in reverse: it requires a roadworthy on sale and on certain registrations, not annually.

## The order to do things in

Going to Victoria: book the VicRoads appointment first, while the New South Wales registration is still current. Attend with plates, form, identity documents and a screwdriver. Pay registration, TAC and plates. Then lodge form 1565 with Service NSW for the motor vehicle tax refund, and ring your green slip insurer.

Coming to New South Wales: blue slip first, because it expires in 42 days and everything else hangs off it. Green slip second. Service NSW third, with the Victorian plates and your Victorian certificate of registration for the duty exemption. Cancel the Victorian registration through myVicRoads last, using the receipt Service NSW gives you.

Two dates decide most of the cost: the day your current registration expires, and the day the blue slip or the VicRoads appointment lands. Get those in the right order and the rest is queueing. Get them wrong and you are paying for an inspection twice, or driving something a highway patrol car can defect on the Lincoln Causeway. If you need a workshop on either side before you start, the directory lists [mechanics in Albury](/nsw/albury/mechanics/), [mechanics in Wodonga](/vic/wodonga/mechanics/) and [inspection stations](/categories/vehicle-inspections/) across the border region.

## Sources

Checked on 2026-08-25. Government fees and rules are indexed and revised, so open the source before you rely on a figure.
